alerts.title: AKI likely pre-renal, not TDF toxicity
alerts.message: Guidelines list TDF as a cause of acute kidney injury requiring LFTs and RFTs when deranged. Patient has creatinine 2.4 (from 0.9) on TDF. However, strong evidence favours pre-renal AKI from gastroenteritis: 5 days vomiting and diarrhoea, hypotension (90/60), tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, urea:creatinine ratio 24:1, and urinalysis showing no protein or glucose. TDF nephrotoxicity typically presents with proximal tubular dysfunction (proteinuria, glycosuria). Two household contacts share the same illness. Stopping TDF permanently may be unnecessary if renal function recovers with rehydration.

evidence.recommended_action: Continue IV fluid resuscitation and recheck creatinine after rehydration before deciding on permanent TDF discontinuation. If creatinine normalises, TDF can likely be continued.

alerts.title: TDF monitoring during acute kidney injury
alerts.message: Guidelines require serum creatinine monitoring for patients on TDF. The patient has severe AKI (creatinine 2.4, from baseline 0.9) while continuing TDF. Even if pre-renal in origin, TDF should be held temporarily during significant acute kidney injury to avoid compounding nephrotoxicity, especially with concurrent dehydration and hypokalaemia (K+ 3.1). The clinician's plan does not include temporary TDF interruption or a timeline for renal re-evaluation before a permanent switch decision.

evidence.recommended_action: Hold TDF temporarily during AKI and dehydration. Recheck renal function after rehydration. Resume TDF if creatinine returns to baseline; switch to TAF-based regimen if it does not.

alerts.title: Hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia need correction
alerts.message: Patient has hypokalaemia (K+ 3.1 mmol/L) and hyponatraemia (Na+ 132 mmol/L) secondary to severe gastroenteritis with dehydration. Potassium 3.1 mmol/L is moderate hypokalaemia and poses arrhythmia risk, especially with tachycardia (pulse 112). The clinician's plan addresses IV fluid resuscitation but does not explicitly include potassium replacement or electrolyte monitoring. TDF can cause renal tubular dysfunction leading to electrolyte wasting, though the absent proteinuria and glycosuria make gastroenteritis the more likely cause.

evidence.recommended_action: Add potassium replacement to IV fluids and monitor electrolytes closely. Recheck sodium and potassium after initial resuscitation.
